findings.statement: CXCR2 is the top convergence candidate: up in all eight cohorts (meta log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.814]), Open Targets association score [gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5345], and small-molecule antagonists in the clinic (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin, danirixin, elubrixin, SX-682). Reactome places it in neutrophil degranulation and chemokine receptor signalling. It has no cis-pQTL or gut eQTL instrument, so MR is not tested (not evidence against).

CXCL8 (the ligand of CXCR1 and CXCR2, with a very high-confidence STRING link to CXCR2) is strongly up (meta log2FC [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.864]) in all eight cohorts, but has no Open Targets genetic association and its plasma-protein MR is null (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]). The signal is expression/inflammation-led, not genetically supported; anti-CXCL8 antibodies reached only phase two.

CXCL5 is up in biopsies, yet plasma-protein MR is significant in the opposite direction: higher protein lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CXCL5; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.634]), using a tag variant and without colocalisation with the IBD GWAS. Blood genetics therefore do not support blocking this chemokine axis and the signal may come from a neighbouring variant.

CD274 (PD-L1) is up in the biopsies but plasma-protein MR shows higher protein lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]) with colocalisation to an IBD GWAS signal. It looks like a protective feedback response, so PD-L1 inhibitors (approved in oncology) would be expected to be unfavourable; agonism would be the direction suggested. No gut eQTL instrument.

IL12B is the top known UC target by Open Targets (association score [gene=IL12B; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7424]) and the strongest plasma MR hit: higher protein raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]) with colocalisation, supporting the existing inhibition of the IL-12 and IL-23 axis (ustekinumab). It is a positive control for the MR design.

JAK2 has the second-highest Open Targets association score ([gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) and drugs in the clinic, but it changes only modestly in biopsies (small meta effect, lower expression component) and has no MR instrument. It is genetically/known-target supported rather than expression-led.

IDO1 is strongly up (meta log2FC [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.118]) in all eight cohorts with inhibitors in the clinic (epacadostat, linrodostat), but there is no Open Targets genetic association and plasma MR is null (p [gene=IDO1; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.111]); colon eQTL is also not significant. Tryptophan catabolism is the Reactome pathway.

FCGR2A has a high Open Targets genetic association score ([gene=FCGR2A; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5543]) and is up in biopsies, but plasma MR is null (p [gene=FCGR2A; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.68]) and the gut cell-type test is also not significant; it has no drug in Open Targets. The expression change likely reflects infiltrating myeloid cells.

IL2RA has genetic association and approved/clinical drugs (basiliximab, aldesleukin), but plasma MR is null (p [gene=IL2RA; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.237]) and colon eQTL MR is also not significant, so genetic causality for UC is not shown in these layers.

CHI3L1 is among the largest and most replicated biopsy increases (meta log2FC [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.875]) but has no genetic association and no drug; tractability is predicted only. Better suited as a biomarker than a target.
SLC26A3 is down in biopsies and has Open Targets genetic association with no drug; epithelial transporter loss is a genetically supported tissue-change marker rather than an inhibitable target.

caveats: Plasma MR is not tissue MR; many top candidates (CXCR2, JAK2, CXCL8 colon) have no instrument, which is not evidence against them.
Strongest gut eQTL hits (for example IRF8, IRF5, GSDMA and GSDMB) are not among the top expression-ranked genes, so blood/gut genetics and biopsy expression largely identify different genes.
Drug lists come from Open Targets and include trials in other indications; none is shown to be tested in UC here.
Genetically supported genes that barely change in biopsies (JAK2, FCGR2A, IL2RA) may act through immune cells or be diluted in bulk tissue.
